title: “Medium Roast, Cream, No Plastic”: New Coffee Cup Coating Protects Against Microplastics - Nautilus
gist: University of Waterloo chemists, after finding polyethylene-lined paper cups degrade and shed particles, developed a plant-based cellulose acetate/cellulose nanocrystal cup coating (ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering) aimed at cutting microplastics and easing recycling.

insights.claim: Paper coffee cups are typically lined with a thin polyethylene coating that may shed microplastics, and the paper-plastic mix makes them hard to recycle, so many likely end up in landfill.
insights.so_what: Regulatory pressure on single-use packaging could favor substitutes to PE-lined cups.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: Americans use roughly 136 million disposable cups each day, by some estimates.
insights.so_what: Sizes the addressable market for alternative cup coatings.
insights.quote: Americans use roughly 136 million of these disposable cups each day
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: University of Waterloo chemists found polyethylene-coated cups experience surface degradation and particle release, and developed a plant-based waterproof barrier of cellulose acetate infused with cellulose nanocrystals, published in ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering.
insights.so_what: Watch for commercialization by packaging makers; cellulose-based barriers are a potential PE-liner replacement.
insights.quote: a plant-based protective barrier made of cellulose acetate infused with cellulose nanocrystals
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
